subtitle: Moha Mudgara — first 20 verses
poet_note: with verses of the disciples after the first twelve
intro: Shankara’s hammer of delusion: seek Govinda, not grammar, wealth, or the body. The first twelve verses are his; a colophon follows, then verses of the disciples. This page is the first twenty of the usual recension. The refrain भज गोविन्दं is sung after each verse; here it stands as verse 1.

sa: when it is close at hand
en: Worship Govinda, worship Govinda, O deluded mind.
When the hour of death is upon you, the rules of grammar will not save you.
stanzas.note: The story: Shankara meets an aged scholar in Varanasi drilling Pāṇini. डुकृङ्करणे is a technical grammar formula, standing here for mere book-learning.

sa: earned by your own past deeds
en: O fool, give up the thirst to pile up wealth; set the mind on wisdom and on freedom from craving.
Whatever comes through your own past work — with that, content the heart.

sa: this is a modification of flesh, fat, and the like
en: Seeing a woman’s breasts and navel, do not fall into the spell of delusion.
Think again and again: this is only a change of flesh and fat.

sa: seized by disease and by pride
en: Water on a lotus leaf trembles and will not stay; life in this world is just as restless.
Know the whole world as seized by sickness and pride, and struck by sorrow.

sa: so long as one is busy earning wealth
en: While a man can still earn, the household gathers round him with affection.
When the body is worn out, no one at home even asks how he is.
While breath still lives in the body, the household asks after one’s welfare.
When the breath has gone, even the wife shrinks from the corpse.

sa: the child is absorbed in play
the youth is absorbed in a young woman
the old man is absorbed in worry
en: Childhood is lost in play; youth is lost in the beloved.
Old age is lost in worry. Almost no one is lost in the Supreme Brahman.
Who is your wife? Who is your son? This round of birth and death is a strange play.
Whose are you? Who are you? From where have you come? Brother, think on that here.

sa: from the company of the good
en: Good company gives rise to non-attachment; non-attachment, to freedom from delusion.
That freedom becomes a still truth — and from that stillness, liberation in this very life.
stanzas.note: A chain of cause: satsaṅga → nissaṅgatva → nirmoha → niścala-tattva → jīvanmukti.

en: When youth is gone, what is lust? When the water is gone, what is a lake?
When wealth is gone, what is family? When Truth is known, what is saṃsāra?

sa: Time, in the blink of an eye
this entire (world) is made of māyā
en: Do not take pride in wealth, in people, or in youth: Time steals them in a blink.
Leave this world of māyā; know the state of Brahman, and enter it.

sa: does one let go the gale of desire
en: Day and night, evening and morning, winter and spring return again.
Time plays, life runs out — and still one does not drop the storm of wanting.

sa: the company of the good, alone
for crossing the ocean of becoming
en: Why this worry over beloved and wealth, O madman? Have you no one to steer you?
In all three worlds, only the company of the good is the boat across the ocean of birth and death.

sa: this teaching was given, by those skilled in knowledge
en: In these twelve flower-clusters the whole counsel has been spoken to the grammarian.
The teaching came from the blessed Śaṅkara, master of knowledge, whose refuge is the Lord.
stanzas.note: Colophon of the first twelve verses (the dvādaśa-mañjarikā), Shankara’s own. The verses that follow are traditionally those of his disciples.

sa: for the sake of the belly
en: Matted hair, shaven head, plucked hair, ochre cloth — so many costumes.
The fool looks and still does not see: these disguises are for the belly’s sake.

sa: does he let go the lump of hope
en: The body is wasted, the head grey, the mouth without teeth.
The old man walks with a staff — and still he will not drop the lump of hope.

sa: alms, and dwelling under a tree
does he let go the noose of desire
en: Fire in front, sun at the back; at night the chin is tucked on the knees.
Alms in the palm, a tree for a house — and still the noose of desire is not cut.

sa: a pilgrimage to the Ganga’s mouth
en: One may go to Gaṅgā-sāgara, keep vows, or give gifts.
Without knowledge, say all the schools, liberation does not come in a hundred births.

sa: the bare earth, and a deerskin
en: A dwelling at a temple tree, the earth for a bed, a deerskin for cloth.
Giving up every possession and pleasure — whom does dispassion not make glad?
Whether given to yoga or to pleasure, to company or to solitude —
the one whose mind delights in Brahman rejoices, rejoices, rejoices indeed.
stanzas.note: Traditionally attributed to Nityānanda. The hymn continues beyond this verse in the usual 31-verse recension.
